newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-EMI reveals toolbox for Euro central bank.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMI reveals toolbox for Euro central bank.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute, the forerunner to the European Central Bank, on Friday unveiled its design for the toolkit which will ensure that Europe has a strong credible monetary policy from 1999.

In a report published in Frankfurt, the EMI revealed a set of monetary policy instruments for the future central bank, but made clear that the final decisions on several key outstanding issues would have to be made by the ECB itself.
The new central bank, which will take over monetary policy responsibility as soon as the European single currency is launched in 1999, will not be up and running until sometime next year.

The report shows that the new central bank will use monetary policy instruments which are similar to those of the German Bundesbank, but with some notable differences in the details of the instruments available.

It will offer funds to banks at two main rates which will set the floor and ceiling for money market rates, similar to the role performed by the Bundesbank's Lombard and discount rates. Open market operations will be its main policy tool.
The report left the decision on the issue of exactly what form of policy strategy the ECB will adopt, but recommended targeting either inflation or the money supply.
It said it had considered five possible monetary strategies that the ECB could adopt, and had eliminated the possibility of exchange rate targeting, interest rate pegging or nominal income targeting.
It said these three did not fit in with the general principles it had set for the ECB's strategy.

"Taking into account a number of guiding principles...and considering the environment likely to prevail in the euro area, the list of potential candidate strategies has been narrowed down to two, namely monetary targeting and direct inflation targeting," the EMI said.
The EMI noted that the Maastricht Treaty made absolutely clear that the ECB had to make price stability its top priority.
"As regards the final objective itself, the Treaty provides unambiguous guidance that 'the primary objective of the ESCB shall be to maintain price stability'," it said.

It also left open the question of whether the European Central Bank would use minimum reserves -- which require banks to deposit some funds at the central bank -- in its policy. The Bundesbank has pushed hard for the inclusion of this instrument.
